reasons: Only 16 of 55 sections were included in this review, so the rest of the file was not checked.
No test or validation for the data was visible.
Lithium is defined in two places, so the copies can drift apart.

terms.meaning: A structured classification, a tree of categories and sub-categories.
A short, URL-friendly name that acts as a unique id for an industry.
The two status labels. STUB appears to mean partial data, but the code does not define it.
The ordered steps an product or service passes through, from raw input to end use.
Million tonnes per year, a common measure of plant capacity.

sections.name: File setup, IndustryStatus, IndustryStructureType
sections.title: Status and structure labels
sections.what: Defines the two allowed status values, LIVE and STUB, and the two allowed ways an industry's breakdown can be laid out.
sections.why: Likely reason: limits each industry to known values so typos are caught.
sections.watch_out: Any page that reads these values must be updated when a new value is added.

sections.name: IndustryNode
sections.title: Shape of one breakdown branch
sections.what: Describes one box in an industry's breakdown: a name, an optional description, and optional smaller boxes inside it.
sections.why: Likely reason: the nested design lets the breakdown go several levels deep.

sections.name: Industry
sections.title: Shape of one industry record
sections.what: Lists the fields every industry needs, such as name, sector, status, breakdown and key metrics, plus optional project count and taxonomy note.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed shape means every industry record has the same fields for pages to read.
sections.watch_out: Project count and taxonomy note are optional, so pages must handle them being missing.

sections.name: SECTORS
sections.title: The six top-level sectors
sections.what: Lists the six sector groups, such as Energy and Power, that industries are placed under, each with a short tagline.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed list gives the pages a consistent set of sector headings.
sections.watch_out: Each industry's sector field must match one of these ids exactly, or it will not be grouped.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_FIRMS
sections.title: Consulting sources behind the taxonomy
sections.what: Builds the list of consulting firm sources the classification is based on, adds the brand's own sources, and writes the one-line note that credits them.
sections.why: Likely reason: the note shows where the classification came from so readers can judge it.
sections.watch_out: The note is written from the last item in the list, so an empty list would produce a broken sentence.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 1)
sections.title: Nuclear power record, first part
sections.what: Starts the industries list and defines the nuclear power record: its name, description, live status, and the first parts of its breakdown, from uranium mining through reactor construction.
sections.why: Likely reason: each industry is kept as readable data so a new one can be added without code changes.
sections.watch_out: This is hand-typed reference data, so a misspelled name or wrong vendor will appear on screen as fact.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 2)
sections.title: Nuclear finish and oil and gas record
sections.what: Finishes the nuclear breakdown, then defines oil and gas as six flat segments, such as offshore field development and refining.
sections.why: Likely reason: oil and gas has no layered value chain, so it uses one flat list and records value-chain position per project, as its note says.
sections.watch_out: Value-chain position is stored per project, so pages must read that field rather than this list.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 3)
sections.title: LNG and gas infrastructure record
sections.what: Defines LNG as a chain from liquefaction through shipping, regasification and storage, with key metrics such as capacity in million tonnes per year.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Metric units are only labels, so nothing stops a value being entered in the wrong unit.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 4)
sections.title: Renewables record, first part
sections.what: Defines renewables and storage with solar, onshore wind, offshore wind, hydropower, and geothermal groups, each with several sized variants.
sections.why: Likely reason: the sub-groups separate technologies that have different costs and project types.
sections.watch_out: Size and depth limits such as 100 MW or 40 m are typed as text and are not checked.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 5)
sections.title: Renewables finish and power grid start
sections.what: Finishes geothermal and battery storage in renewables, then starts the power transmission and grid record with HVDC links, AC lines and substations.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Many records use the same shared taxonomy note, so editing that note changes all of them.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 6)
sections.title: Grid, distribution and hydrogen record
sections.what: Finishes the grid record with smart grid and distribution items such as smart meters and EV charging, then defines hydrogen with production, storage and end-use paths. Hydrogen is marked STUB.
sections.why: Likely reason: STUB seems to mark an industry with partial data, but the code does not say so.
sections.watch_out: Hydrogen is marked STUB, so pages may show it as unfinished. Check the status field before relying on it.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 7)
sections.title: Hydrogen end and mining record start
sections.what: Finishes the hydrogen metrics, then starts the mining and metals record with critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths, each split into sub-groups.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Lithium appears here and also as its own separate industry record, so the two copies can drift apart.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 8)
sections.title: Rare earths, graphite and base metals
sections.what: Lists rare earth, graphite and other critical mineral routes, then starts base metals with copper and aluminum process routes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Process names are free text, so any page that matches on them must use the exact wording.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 9)
sections.title: Zinc, lead, precious metals and steel
sections.what: Lists zinc and lead routes, then gold, silver and platinum group metals, then iron and steel routes from ore to finished steel.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 10)
sections.title: Coal, lithium and gas power records
sections.what: Lists coal mining and processing, defines the separate lithium mining industry, and defines gas-fired power with combined cycle, peaking, cogeneration, steam and coal-to-gas conversion.
sections.why: Likely reason: gas power notes that records with no asset class get no sub-industry, rather than an invented one.
sections.watch_out: The lithium list here repeats the one inside mining and metals, so update both if the routes change.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 11)
sections.title: Chemicals record and industrial gases start
sections.what: Defines chemicals and petrochemicals as a STUB with olefins and polymers, aromatics and polyester, fertilizers, and specialty chemicals, then starts industrial gases.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Chemicals is marked STUB, so treat its lists as a starting point rather than a complete picture.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 12)
sections.title: Closes gases entry, opens dairy plants
sections.what: Finishes the category list of an earlier industry, which covers air separation, hydrogen, and carbon capture. It then starts the Dairy Processing entry with its name, description, and first three plant types: fluid milk, cheese, and butter and ghee. Each plant type lists its specific processes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the very long industry list is split across many sections for readability. Reason for the dairy design not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The dairy taxonomy note is cut off in the source, so its full text cannot be read here.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 13)
sections.title: Dairy plant types continued
sections.what: Adds more dairy plant types: yogurt, milk powder, whey and protein concentrate, casein, ice cream, and the start of infant formula. Each plant type lists its processes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The pattern groups dairy plants by what they make.
sections.watch_out: Plant type names here must match the citation keys in the citations section exactly, or the sources will not show.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 14)
sections.title: Dairy plant types and value chain
sections.what: Finishes infant formula and adds condensed milk, cream and desserts, plant-based alternatives, and the upstream farm, cold chain, and by-products groups. The last three are farm, shipping, and waste-handling items rather than processing plants.
sections.why: Likely reason: the taxonomy note says the farm, cold chain, and by-product groups are included for full project visibility. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The taxonomy note says these last three groups may later be split into their own industries, so their location could change.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 15)
sections.title: Dairy key metrics, rail begins
sections.what: Closes the dairy entry and sets the dairy key figures shown to users: capacity in millions of liters per year, plant type, operator, and startup year. Then opens the Rail and Transit entry with high-speed rail and metro.
sections.why: Key metrics tell the reader which numbers matter for each industry. Reason for these exact choices not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Key metric labels are shown on screen, so a change here changes what users see.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 16)
sections.title: Rail stations and depots
sections.what: Finishes the rail list with stations and depots, covering mega-station redevelopment and heavy maintenance depots. Then opens the Ports and Maritime entry with container terminals, bulk terminals, and shipyards.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each rail group sorts projects by type of asset.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 17)
sections.title: Ports entry and water utilities
sections.what: Finishes the ports list with shipyards and waterway categories, then sets the ports key figures. Then adds the whole Water and Wastewater entry: desalination, wastewater treatment, dams, and bulk water transfer.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Entries follow the same pattern as the others.
sections.watch_out: Ports and water entries are marked STUB. The code does not say what STUB means, but it likely marks a placeholder with little content.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 18)
sections.title: Real estate categories begin
sections.what: Adds the Real Estate entry and its first categories: residential, retail, office, hospitality and leisure, and the first part of industrial and logistics.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Real estate is listed as a live industry, so these categories are meant to be shown to users.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 19)
sections.title: Real estate ends, data centers start
sections.what: Finishes the industrial and logistics group, then adds mixed-use districts. Then opens the Data Centers entry with hyperscale campuses, colocation, and edge sites.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Groups follow a fixed pattern of a name, a short description, and child items.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 20)
sections.title: Subsea cables and terrestrial fiber
sections.what: Finishes the data center list with subsea cables and land-based fiber backbones, and sets the data center key figures. Then opens the Semiconductor Fabs entry with wafer fabrication and assembly, test, and packaging.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each category separates a different stage of the business.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 21)
sections.title: Semiconductor equipment and materials
sections.what: Finishes the semiconductor list with equipment makers, chemical suppliers, and silicon wafer plants, then sets its key figures. Then opens the EV and Battery entry with materials refining, cathode and anode materials, and cell manufacturing.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The list follows the order of how a chip or battery is made.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 22)
sections.title: Battery packs and recycling
sections.what: Finishes the battery pack list with cell-to-chassis integration and stationary storage, then adds recycling and second-life items. Then opens the Aerospace and Defense entry with naval shipbuilding, aircraft, and the first missile items.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The grouping follows the battery value chain.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 23)
sections.title: Missiles, space, and list end
sections.what: Finishes the missile group, adds space infrastructure such as launch vehicles and satellite factories, and sets the defense key figures. Then closes the main list of industries.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The closing marks the end of the list that the app reads.
sections.watch_out: New industries must be added before this closing, or they will be left out of the list.

sections.name: getIndustry
sections.title: Look up one industry
sections.what: Given a slug such as dairy or rail-transit, returns the matching industry, or nothing if no match exists. Pages use this to find the industry they show.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app uses short web names (slugs) to open a specific industry page. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Callers must handle the case where nothing is found, or an unknown slug will break the page.

sections.name: getIndustriesBySector
sections.title: List industries in one sector
sections.what: Given a sector id, returns every industry that belongs to that sector, in list order. An unknown sector returns an empty list.
sections.why: Likely reason: sectors group industries on pages such as the home page. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: An unknown sector id gives an empty list without any error, so a typo looks like a missing sector.

sections.name: countAllNodes
sections.title: Count every category in a tree
sections.what: Counts all categories and sub-categories in a tree, including the top-level ones and all their children. A missing list counts as zero.
sections.why: Likely reason: used to show how big an industry's structure is. Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: countLeafNodes
sections.title: Count only final items
sections.what: Counts only the bottom-level items, those with no children, across a tree. A missing list counts as zero.
sections.why: Likely reason: final items are the specific project types, so this gives a count of real categories. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The count of final items will be smaller than the count of all categories, so the two numbers must not be mixed up.

sections.name: SourceType
sections.title: Allowed kinds of source
sections.what: Lists the seven allowed types of source: industry association, consulting firm, trade publication, government, academic, vendor, and intergovernmental body.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app show where a source comes from and how much weight it carries. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Any new source kind must be added here first, or the code will not accept it.

sections.name: TaxonomySource
sections.title: Shape of a publisher record
sections.what: Describes one publisher: its id, short name, full name, kind, authority level from 1 to 3, optional country, and a short description.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The record gives the reader a clear source for each citation.
sections.watch_out: The authority level is a plain number. The code does not say whether 1 is the strongest, so this meaning should be confirmed before judging sources by it.

sections.name: TaxonomyDocument
sections.title: Shape of a publication record
sections.what: Describes one publication: its id, the publisher id it belongs to, title, optional year, optional link, and optional format such as report or handbook.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. A separate publication record lets many citations point to the same document.
sections.watch_out: The publisher id must match a publisher record, or the link to the source breaks without any warning.

sections.name: QuoteType
sections.title: How closely a quote matches
sections.what: Defines three labels that show how close a citation is to its source: verbatim (exact words), paraphrased (close rewording), and summary (the editor's view).
sections.why: Likely reason: makes the difference between exact quotes and rewording visible to readers. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The code cannot check which label is correct. Someone must set each label by hand, so an incorrect label goes unnoticed.

sections.name: TaxonomyCitation
sections.title: Shape of one citation
sections.what: Describes one citation: the document id, the excerpt text, the quote label, and optional section number, link, and note.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each citation explains why a plant type or category is classified the way it is.
sections.watch_out: The document id must match a publication record, or the citation will not link to any source.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 1)
sections.title: Dairy and whey publisher records
sections.what: Records the publishers for dairy and whey: the International Dairy Federation, the US dairy foods association, the European dairy association, the US milk producers, Dairy Australia, and the American Whey Institute.
sections.why: Likely reason: the dairy citations need named sources to point to. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Each record is saved under a key name and also has an id field. The two must match, or lookups will fail quietly.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 2)
sections.title: Whey, equipment, and government sources
sections.what: Adds the European whey processors, the equipment makers Tetra Pak, GEA, and SPX FLOW, and the US dairy agency records.
sections.why: Likely reason: equipment makers publish the plant layouts that the dairy classifications follow. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Records are found only by their exact key. A typo in a key quietly returns nothing.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 3)
sections.title: Government and consulting publishers
sections.what: Adds the US economic research agency, Eurostat, and Codex Alimentarius, then the consulting firms McKinsey, BCG, PwC, and KPMG.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Government bodies and consulting firms are used as independent references.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 4)
sections.title: More consulting, trade, and mining sources
sections.what: Adds Deloitte, EY, and the brand sources pulled in from another file. Then adds dairy trade magazines and the US Geological Survey and the energy agency.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The brand sources are kept in a separate file, probably to keep this list shorter.
sections.watch_out: Keys defined later in an object replace earlier keys with the same name. The brand sources come from another file, so a clash could silently replace an entry here.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 5)
sections.title: Nuclear and last sources
sections.what: Adds the energy agency's critical minerals work, the nuclear agency, and the World Nuclear Association. Then closes the sources list.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These entries support the mining and nuclear classifications.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 1)
sections.title: First publication records
sections.what: Opens the publications list and records the first items: the Tetra Pak handbook, the whey standards manual, an international dairy bulletin, two Codex standards, Eurostat's classification, the US dairy data, and a dairy trade report.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each record gives a title, year, and link to the original.
sections.watch_out: Links and years are typed in by hand. The code does not check that they still work or are correct.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 2)
sections.title: More publication records
sections.what: Adds dairy economic reports, a whey production factsheet, an equipment brochure, a membrane guide, and consulting reports from McKinsey, PwC, and BCG.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Gathering the documents in one place lets many citations share them.
sections.watch_out: Links and years are typed in by hand and are not checked by the code.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 3)
sections.title: Final publication records
sections.what: Adds a construction survey, the energy agency's critical minerals outlook, the US minerals summary, the nuclear reactor database, and the small reactor library entry. Then closes the publications list.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These documents back the mining and nuclear citations.
sections.watch_out: Links are typed in by hand and are not checked by the code.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 1)
sections.title: Dairy citations begin
sections.what: Opens the citation map, which is keyed first by industry and then by category name. It then adds the first dairy citations, for fluid milk, cheese, butter and ghee, and yogurt. Each has a quote and a link to its source.
sections.why: Likely reason: the citations show users why each category exists. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Category names are matched exactly. Renaming a category in the industry list silently removes its citations, because the lookup returns an empty list.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 2)
sections.title: Yogurt and powder citations
sections.what: Finishes the yogurt citations and adds citations for milk powder and the first whey protein category.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each citation points to a specific document.
sections.watch_out: Excerpt wording is written by hand, and the code cannot check it against the source.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 3)
sections.title: Whey citations and protein grades
sections.what: Adds citations for whey processing, protein concentrate grades, protein isolate, hydrolysate, native whey, and demineralized whey.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The whey groups have the most citations, which suggests they needed the most explanation.
sections.watch_out: Category names such as the concentrate grades must match the industry list exactly, including spaces and slashes.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 4)
sections.title: Casein, ice cream, and formula citations
sections.what: Finishes the demineralized whey citations, then adds citations for casein, ice cream, infant formula, and plant-based alternatives.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each category gets at least one source.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 5)
sections.title: Mining citations begin
sections.what: Adds a second industry group for mining and metals, with citations for lithium and critical minerals.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. This group uses the same citation pattern as dairy.
sections.watch_out: Some category names here, such as the critical minerals one, do not appear in the structure shown in this packet, so those citations may never be used.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 6)
sections.title: Lithium and nuclear citations, end of map
sections.what: Adds lithium mining citations and nuclear reactor citations, then closes the citation map.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These cover the same source types as the earlier groups.
sections.watch_out: The same quote text is repeated under several categories. Editing one copy will not change the others, so the copies can drift apart.

sections.name: getDocument
sections.title: Find a publication
sections.what: Given a publication id, returns that publication record, or nothing if none exists.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets a citation find its document. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: An unknown id returns nothing, so the caller must handle that case.

sections.name: getSource
sections.title: Find a publisher
sections.what: Given a publisher id, returns that publisher record, or nothing if none exists.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets a document find its publisher. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: An unknown id returns nothing, so the caller must handle that case.

sections.name: getCitations
sections.title: Get citations for one category
sections.what: Given an industry and a category name, returns that category's citations. If nothing matches, returns an empty list.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets a page show the sources behind one category. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: An empty list hides a name mismatch, so a missing citation can look like a category with no sources.

sections.name: getIndustryTaxonomySources
sections.title: Collect all sources for one industry
sections.what: Given an industry, gathers every publisher behind its citations, with no repeats. Citations that point to a missing publication are skipped.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets an industry page list all its sources in one place. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Skipped citations are not reported, so a broken link can drop a source from the list without any warning.

summary: Holds the reference data for the industries the toolkit covers: their names, sectors, status, breakdowns, and the consulting sources behind the classification.
purpose: Stores the industry list and its source material as data, so the pages can show it without hardcoded text.
why: Likely reason: keeping the classification in one data file lets it be updated without changing page layouts.
how: First defines the status and structure labels and the sector list. Then builds the shared taxonomy note from the consulting firm list. Then lists each industry as a record with its breakdown. The file ends with the taxonomy sources, documents and citations, and small lookup helpers such as getIndustry and getIndustriesBySector.
inputs: No live inputs. It reads the brand lists BRAND_TAXONOMY_FIRMS and BRAND_TAXONOMY_SOURCES from the brand file.
outputs: Exported lists of industries, sectors, taxonomy sources, documents and citations, plus lookup helpers that return one industry or a filtered list.
risks: The data is typed by hand, so a typo, a wrong sector id, or a duplicated record shows up on screen as fact. The lithium data is also stored twice.
debug: If an industry is missing or in the wrong group, check its sector id against the sectors list. If a note looks wrong, check the shared taxonomy note and the firm list. If a lookup returns nothing, check the slug spelling.
